entities.name: John of Falkenberg
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John of Falkenberg (Johannes Falkenberg), a German Dominican theologian, emerged as a highly controversial figure during the early 15th century, particularly known for his incendiary theological polemics against the Kingdom of Poland-Lithuania at the Council of Constance. His writings, which notoriously equated the Polish monarchy with the Antichrist, underscore the intense political and religious conflicts that characterized the decline of the High Middle Ages and the rise of nascent national identities within the Holy Roman Empire and Eastern Europe.

Serving as a delegate for the Teutonic Knights, Falkenberg penned his most infamous work, *De Doctrina et Vita Antichristi*, around 1416 during the Council of Constance (1414-1418). In this treatise, he not only accused King Władysław II Jagiełło of Poland and his kingdom of heresy and paganism but also argued for the permissibility, even necessity, of assassinating the Polish monarch and subjugating his people. This extreme position was a direct response to the Teutonic Order's devastating defeat by Polish-Lithuanian forces at the Battle of Grunwald (Tannenberg) in 1410, seeking to delegitimize their Christian opponents through theological means.

Falkenberg's radical views, far from being universally embraced, were met with severe condemnation. The Council of Constance itself, despite its broader mission of healing the Great Schism and combating heresy, found his doctrines too extreme, especially given Poland's recent conversion of Lithuania and its status as a Christian kingdom. He was subsequently imprisoned by order of the Council, where he remained until his death around 1430, a testament to the theological limits even in an era of intense religious-political maneuvering.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: John of Falkenberg's extreme theological polemics at the Council of Constance, though condemned, significantly illustrate the use of religious rhetoric to justify political and military conflict in late medieval Europe, particularly concerning the Teutonic Order's struggle against Poland-Lithuania. His case marked a boundary for acceptable theological discourse, even during a period of intense church reform.
